mcqs.question: In a fully-sorted matrix with n columns, a flat index k maps to which (row, col) position?
options: row = k % n, col = k // n
row = k // n, col = k % n
row = k, col = n - k
row and col cannot be recovered without materializing the flattened array
mcqs.explanation: Integer division by the column count n gives the row (how many full rows of n elements fit before index k), and the remainder gives the position within that row — no separate flattened array copy is needed. The other formulas don't correspond to a valid row-major index mapping.

mcqs.question: The flat-index binary search for a fully-sorted matrix reuses the same template as ordinary 1D binary search. What is the ONLY addition needed?
options: A completely different loop structure with two nested binary searches
Translating the flat index mid into a (row, col) position on each comparison, via mid // n and mid % n
Sorting the matrix again before searching
A separate pass to build an actual flattened 1D array first
mcqs.explanation: Since a fully-sorted matrix behaves exactly like a 1D sorted array, the search logic itself is unchanged from ordinary binary search — the only addition is converting the flat index into a 2D position to actually read the value, done on the fly rather than via a separate array-building pass. No nested loops or re-sorting are needed.

mcqs.question: A matrix has each row sorted left-to-right and each column sorted top-to-bottom, but no guarantee about how values in one row compare to another row. Why does flat-index binary search fail here?
options: It doesn't fail — this matrix type is identical to a fully-sorted matrix
Flat-index binary search only fails when the matrix is not square
It fails only because the matrix has more rows than columns
Reading the matrix row by row does not produce a single sorted sequence, since values in later rows can be smaller than values in earlier rows, violating binary search's core invariant
mcqs.explanation: Without a guarantee tying rows together, concatenating rows can produce a sequence that rises and falls arbitrarily between rows, which is exactly the condition binary search's invariant depends on NOT happening — the target could easily be excluded from consideration incorrectly. This has nothing to do with the matrix being square or the relative row/column counts, and it's a fundamentally different structure from the fully-sorted case, not an identical one.

mcqs.question: Why does the staircase search specifically start at the TOP-RIGHT corner of a row-and-column-sorted matrix?
options: It's an arbitrary choice — any corner works identically
The top-right corner always holds the maximum value in the matrix
It's the only position where a single comparison against the target can eliminate an entire row or an entire column outright
Starting there guarantees the search finishes in exactly one step
mcqs.explanation: From the top-right corner, a too-large value rules out its whole column (everything below is even larger), and a too-small value rules out its whole row (everything to the left is even smaller) — that dual elimination property only holds from a corner where one direction increases and the other decreases, which is top-right (or symmetrically bottom-left), not an arbitrary starting point. It's not necessarily the matrix's maximum, and the search generally takes multiple steps, not exactly one.

mcqs.question: Why does the staircase search cost O(m+n) rather than the O(log(mn)) that flat-index binary search achieves on a fully-sorted matrix?
options: Each staircase step eliminates only one row or one column at a time, never a fraction of the remaining search space, so the total steps are bounded by rows plus columns rather than shrinking geometrically
The staircase search is simply an inefficient implementation of the same algorithm
O(m+n) is actually faster than O(log(mn)) for any matrix size
The staircase search re-scans the entire matrix on every step
mcqs.explanation: A row-and-column-sorted matrix lacks the global structure needed for a halving strategy — each step can only rule out one row or column entirely, which bounds the total work linearly in the dimensions rather than logarithmically in the total element count. This is a fundamentally different, weaker guarantee than the fully-sorted case, not an inefficiency in an otherwise-equivalent algorithm, and O(m+n) is generally worse than O(log(mn)) for large matrices, not better.

mcqs.question: A candidate applies flat-index binary search to a matrix that is only row-and-column-sorted (not fully sorted). What's the risk?
options: No risk — the technique works identically on both matrix types
Only a minor performance loss, since the answer will still be found correctly
A genuine correctness bug — the flattened sequence isn't actually sorted, so the search's core invariant is violated and it can converge on a wrong answer or miss the target entirely
The code will fail to compile due to a type mismatch
mcqs.explanation: Since flattening a row-and-column-sorted matrix doesn't produce an actually sorted sequence, binary search's foundational guarantee — that the target, if present, remains within the shrinking window — is broken from the very first comparison, risking a genuinely wrong result, not just wasted time. This is a real correctness failure, and the two matrix types require different techniques specifically because they're structurally different, not interchangeable.
